title: The root of good fortune
hookLine: having searched every room, Hanuman sits down in the dark and considers giving up, and then talks himself back up
carry: anirveda: don't let despair make the decision
last: SITA WOULD NOT SLEEP LIKE THIS.

cards: Hanuman has searched Ravana's palace from end to end, room after room, and he hasn't found her. The night is wearing on. He has reached the end of the list, and he sits down.
Sometimes the hardest moment isn't the danger; it's that. And Valmiki gives the hero of the Sundara Kanda something surprising here: a full, honest spell of despair.

teach.b: First, a moment of conscience. Hanuman has walked among sleeping women, other men's wives, and looked at them. Has he done wrong?
He thinks it through. His mind, he decides, was not disturbed: a woman must be searched for among women, and his intention was pure. Valmiki lets him weigh it rather than skip it.
Then the despair. Maybe Sita is dead, he thinks. Maybe the rakshasas killed her.
Early in it, Valmiki gives him a line in Sanskrit: anirvedaḥ śriyo mūlam. Not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune. He searches again, cellars, halls, corners.
Still nothing. The despair comes back, deeper. If I go back without news, Rama will die of grief, then Lakshmana, then Bharata, then Rama's mothers, and on through Sugriva.
He follows the chain of sorrow all the way down.
For a while he even thinks of not going back at all, of staying by the sea as a hermit. Then, slowly, he turns.

teach.h: HE GETS UP AND SEARCHES AGAIN.
teach.b: He bows in his heart to Rama and Lakshmana, to Sita, and to the gods, and begins again. The line didn't settle it once and for all. He said it, and still fell further.

It's about what he did next, each time. Despair came and sat with him, and he didn't let it make the decision. This part ends with him looking out from the palace walls at a grove of trees he hasn't entered yet.

how: Some who recite the Sundara Kanda in hard times dwell on Hanuman's despair and recovery here, and on the phrase anirvedaḥ śriyo mūlam, 'not despairing is the root of good fortune'.

o: the place Hanuman searches end to end, then despairs
the hall where Rama's army holds its war council
the grove where Sita sits guarded by rakshasis

games.q: the low point — tap the pairs.

s: Hanuman never doubts he'll find Sita
he sinks into despair and even thinks of not returning.
Hanuman worries he did wrong by looking at sleeping women
he reasons that his mind was undisturbed and his purpose pure.
the line says a strong person never feels despair
it says not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune.

games.q: you're Hanuman. you've searched every room of the palace and found nothing. what now?
o: stay by the sea as a hermit.
remember there are places you haven't searched, and begin again.
games.why: after thinking of both failure and hiding, Hanuman tells himself not to give in to despair, and resumes the search.

practice: If there's something you've been close to giving up on, let it come to mind gently, and don't argue with the discouragement; let it sit beside you, the way Hanuman's despair sat with him. Breathe with it.
Then, on one breath, notice whether there's one place you haven't looked yet, one small next step, and just let it appear.

wordCard.voice: Ravana's palace. Where Hanuman searches every room and finds no Sita, sinks into despair, and rises again: not giving in to despair is the root of good fortune.

orig.note: Sanskrit: 'not despairing (is) the root of good fortune.'

carryVoice: Your line: anirveda, don't let despair make the decision. Even heroes sit down sometimes. Day six hundred fifteen.
